quiz.q: What's the main advantage BTreeMap has over HashMap?
options: Faster average-case insert and lookup
Keys are always kept in sorted order, and it supports efficient range queries
It uses less memory in every case
It doesn't require the Ord trait
quiz.explain: HashMap is faster on average (O(1) vs BTreeMap's O(log n)) but gives no order guarantee. BTreeMap trades some speed for always-sorted keys and range() queries.

quiz.q: What trait must a BTreeMap's key type implement, and why?
options: Hash, same as HashMap
Ord, so the map can compare keys to decide sort position
Copy, so keys can be duplicated
Default, so missing keys get a placeholder
quiz.explain: BTreeMap must always know whether one key is less than, equal to, or greater than another to keep itself sorted — that's exactly what Ord provides.

quiz.q: For a custom struct like `struct Version { major: u32, minor: u32 }`, what does `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]` compare first?
options: The fields in alphabetical order by name
The fields in declaration order — major first, then minor as a tiebreaker
Only the first field, ignoring the rest
It picks a random field each time
quiz.explain: Derived Ord compares struct fields in the order they're declared, using each subsequent field as a tiebreaker — exactly the behavior you want for a version number.

quiz.q: Why is VecDeque faster than Vec for adding elements to the front?
options: VecDeque doesn't actually store elements contiguously in memory at all
VecDeque is a ring buffer, so the logical front can move without shifting every other element; Vec::insert(0, x) has to shift all elements
VecDeque elements are always smaller
Vec cannot have a front at all
quiz.explain: VecDeque treats its buffer as a ring, so push_front is O(1). Vec's elements are always contiguous starting at index 0, so inserting at the front means shifting everything over — O(n).

quiz.q: When should you prefer plain Vec over VecDeque?
options: Never, VecDeque is strictly better
When you only ever push and pop from the back — Vec has slightly less overhead for that access pattern
When you need sorted keys
When you need O(1) lookup by key
quiz.explain: VecDeque's flexibility (fast at both ends) isn't free, and Vec remains the better default when the front is never touched.

quiz.q: By default, what does BinaryHeap::pop() return?
options: The smallest remaining element
The largest remaining element
A random remaining element
The first element pushed, like a queue
quiz.explain: BinaryHeap is a max-heap by default — pop() always hands back the largest element currently in the heap.

quiz.q: How do you get min-heap behavior (smallest first) out of BinaryHeap?
options: Call heap.reverse() before popping
Wrap pushed values in std::cmp::Reverse, then unwrap after popping
BinaryHeap cannot do this; use BTreeSet instead
Pass a comparator argument to BinaryHeap::new()
quiz.explain: Reverse(x) flips what 'greater' means for x, so the heap's largest-by-Reverse-ordering value is really the smallest wrapped value. Push Reverse(x), pop and destructure Reverse(smallest).

quiz.q: Does iterating a BinaryHeap with `for x in &heap` visit elements in largest-to-smallest order?
options: Yes, always
No — only repeated .pop() calls guarantee that order; plain iteration visits elements in unspecified internal order
Only if the heap has fewer than 10 elements
Only for a min-heap built with Reverse
quiz.explain: The heap's internal layout is optimized for pop(), not for a sorted walk. Iterating directly does not guarantee any particular order.

quiz.q: Which collection would you choose for a sliding window that needs to cheaply drop old items from one end while adding new ones to the other?
options: BinaryHeap, because it always has the max ready
VecDeque, because push/pop are O(1) at both front and back
BTreeMap, because keys are sorted
HashSet, because membership checks are fast
quiz.explain: A sliding window adds at one end and removes at the other repeatedly — exactly VecDeque's O(1)-both-ends strength.

flashcards.front: BTreeMap vs HashMap — the core trade-off.
flashcards.back: BTreeMap: keys always sorted, O(log n), supports range queries. HashMap: faster average O(1), but no order guarantee.

flashcards.front: What trait do BTreeMap/BTreeSet keys need?
flashcards.back: Ord (which requires Eq and PartialOrd) — the map needs to compare keys to keep them sorted.

flashcards.front: How does #[derive(Ord)] order a struct's fields?
flashcards.back: By declaration order: the first field is compared first, subsequent fields break ties in the order they're declared.

flashcards.front: What makes VecDeque different from Vec?
flashcards.back: VecDeque is a ring buffer with O(1) push/pop at BOTH ends. Vec is O(1) at the back only — the front requires shifting every element, O(n).

flashcards.front: When should you still prefer Vec over VecDeque?
flashcards.back: When you only ever push/pop the back — Vec has less overhead for that single-ended access pattern.

flashcards.front: What does BinaryHeap::pop() return by default?
flashcards.back: The largest remaining element — BinaryHeap is a max-heap by default.

flashcards.front: How do you build a min-heap using BinaryHeap?
flashcards.back: Wrap each value in std::cmp::Reverse before pushing; std::cmp::Reverse flips the Ord comparison so the 'largest' wrapped value is the smallest real value.

flashcards.front: Does BinaryHeap guarantee sorted order when you iterate it directly (not via pop)?
flashcards.back: No — only repeated .pop() calls guarantee largest-first order. Direct iteration visits elements in unspecified order.
